deep.reconstruction:
CONTEXT. This is a laboratory sheet from the Gauss–Weber earth-inductor (Erdinduktor) experiments in Göttingen, dated 17 July 1836. An earth inductor coil is turned through 180° in the Earth's field. The induced current impulse passes through the multiplier of a magnetometer used as a galvanometer. The resulting swing is read on a scale with mirror and telescope.

A. TIMEKEEPING. Two clocks, 'Shelton' and 'Hardy', are compared three times:
- Shelton 37'50" against Hardy 5h37m50.9s;
- Shelton 26'30" against Hardy 6h26m29.9s;
- Shelton 50'40" against Hardy 6h50m39.3s (the third pair is on the next page).
The offsets Hardy minus Shelton are +0.9, -0.1 and -0.7 s, so the total drift is 1.6 s. The elapsed time is 6:50:39.3 - 5:37:50.9 = 1h12m48.4s = 4368.4 s (written 1.12.48,4 and 43684). The quotient 4368.4/1.6 = 2730.25 gives a relative rate of 1 part in about 2730, i.e. roughly 31.6 s per day. The page shows '2770'; I read it as 2730 or as a slip (my inference). The small numbers 306, 294, 174, 72, 44 are scratch work for this division and are not fully interpretable.

B. TEMPERATURES. Celsius 19.2 is read in the Rotunde (the earth-inductor room) and Réaumur 15.9 at the magnetometer. Later readings are 18.4 °C and 16.3 °R (the next page gives 18.4 | 16.4).

C. REDUCTION OF SWINGS. Each group of three numbers a, b, c is a run of successive turning points of the magnetometer needle in scale divisions. Gauss forms the pair sums a+b and b+c, then their sum S = a+2b+c, which is 4 times the swing centre.

Worked example, block 1. The first reading 1201.0 was struck out; 2339.0 = 1201.0+1138.0 was formed and abandoned. Then:
- 1138.0+1242.5 = 2380.5
- 1242.5+1138.6 = 2381.1
- S1 = 4761.6

The remaining blocks:

| Block | Turning points | Pair sums | S |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2 | 847.7, 897.0, 840.2 | 1744.7, 1737.2 | 3481.9 |
| 3 | 1184.5, 1200.2, 1170.1 | 2384.7, 2370.3 | 4755.0 |
| 4 | 1258.9, 1220.8, 1260.8 | 2479.7, 2481.6 | 4961.3 |
| 5 | 767.7, 816.6, 768.2 | 1584.3, 1584.8 | 3169.1 |
| 6 | 1218.0, 1261.3, 1217.0 | 2479.3, 2478.3 | 4957.6 |
| 7 | 766.2, 812.8, 773.0 | 1579.0, 1585.8 | 3164.8 |

Differences of consecutive S values (4 times the throw):
- 4761.6 - 3481.9 = 1279.7
- mean(4761.6, 4755.0) - 3481.9 = 4758.3 - 3481.9 = 1276.4 (the figure inside the loop drawn around the first blocks; the first blocks seem to have been set aside)
- 4961.3 - 3169.1 = 1792.2
- 4957.6 - 3169.1 = 1788.5
- 4957.6 - 3164.8 = 1792.8

Second-order sums:
- 1792.2 + 1788.5 = 3580.7
- 1788.5 + 1792.8 = 3581.3
- 3580.7 + 3581.3 = 7162.0

This applies the same 1-2-1 weighting again, so 7162.0 is 16 times the mean throw. On the next page Gauss divides: 7162.0/16 = 447.625 scale divisions. This is the elongation produced by the induction impulses for this circuit arrangement.

D. CIRCUIT THEORY (Ohm's law with shunt). Notation: r is the resistance of the inductor circuit, m that of the multiplier, i that of a shunt (Nebenschluss) placed across the multiplier, and E the induced electromotive force.
- Total resistance: R = r + mi/(m+i) = (rm+ri+mi)/(m+i).
- Fraction of the current through the multiplier: i/(m+i).
- Hence I_m = E·i/(rm+ri+mi) = E/(r + m + rm/i). Gauss writes exactly 1/(r+m+rm/i) next to 1/(r+m) and 1/(r+m+i).

Normalised forms with the reference resistance set to 1:
- Series resistance 1 added: I/I0 = (r+m)/(r+m+1) = 1/(1 + 1/(r+m)).
- Shunt i = 1 added: I/I0 = (r+m)/(r+m+rm) = 1/(1 + rm/(r+m)).

Numerically, with r+m = 2.6112 and rm = 1.35116:
- 1 + 1/2.6112 = 1.38296
- 1 + 1.35116/2.6112 = 1.51745

The products 0.51745 × 2.6112 = 1.35117 (and an earlier 1.35109) connect these numbers.

The boxed values are 445.5, 322.1 and 293.6:
- 445.5/1.38296 = 322.13
- 445.5/1.51745 = 293.59
So the box gives the throws expected for three arrangements (normal circuit, extra series unit, unit shunt) from a base value of 445.5. Base value and predictions are nearly consistent with the observed 447.6 and 446.96.

My addition (not on the page): from r+m = 2.6112 and rm = 1.35116, r and m are the roots of x^2 - 2.6112x + 1.35116 = 0, giving about 1.9001 and 0.7111. Which root is r and which is m is not determined here.

The columns '4556 / 19448 / 117', '21664 / 7744 / 25216' and '14201 / 543' are multiplication or division scratch work that I cannot reliably assign.
errors: If the first S-value really reads 4761.8, it is a slip: 2380.5+2381.1 = 4761.6. Gauss's own difference 1279.7 = 4761.6 - 3481.9 shows that 4761.6 was the value used.
'2770' does not equal 4368.4/1.6 = 2730.25; probably a misreading of 2730 or a copying slip.

The boxed 445.5 : 322.1 : 293.6 is not exactly a measured ratio set. 445.5/322.1 = 1.3831 implies r+m = 2.610, not 2.6112. The box is consistent as a prediction from the constants 2.6112 and 1.35116, which suggests those constants came from other data.
Otherwise all pair sums, differences and second-order sums check exactly.

results.what: Reduction of turning points by sums a+2b+c and second-order 1-2-1 combination of differences (divisor 16) to eliminate the decay and drift of the rest position
results.modern_name: Weighted (binomial) mean of turning points for a damped oscillator's equilibrium; finite-difference smoothing

results.what: Clock comparison and rate determination (1.6 s in 1h12m48.4s)
Current through a galvanometer with a shunt: I_m = E/(r+m+rm/i), and the total resistance r + mi/(m+i)
results.modern_name: Ohm's law for a branched circuit (current divider / shunt formula; special case of Kirchhoff's laws)
results.usually_credited_to: Ohm (1827) for the basics; shunt formulas in Pouillet / Wheatstone (1837–43); general network laws Kirchhoff (1845)

results.what: Determination of the relative resistances r+m and rm (hence r and m separately) from throw ratios under an added series unit and a unit shunt
results.modern_name: Resistance determination by series-and-shunt comparison (relative galvanometric method)
results.usually_credited_to: Wheatstone 1843 and Weber's absolute resistance work (1851) for systematic methods

deep.surprise_reason: These are routine laboratory reductions in the known Gauss–Weber induction programme of 1836. The only somewhat notable item is the explicit shunt formula. It is used to separate the inductor and multiplier resistances via series-addition and shunt ratios, about 7 years before Wheatstone's systematic treatment and 9 before Kirchhoff. However, it follows directly from Ohm's law, and Gauss's familiarity with branched circuits is already documented.

transcription_corrections: The partially hidden number inside the drawn loop is 1276.4 (= mean(4761.6, 4755.0) - 3481.9); the transcription omits it.
Header labels: 'Cels. 19,2 Rot[unde]' and 'Reaum. 15,9 Magnetometer' (thermometers), not 'Erdinductor / Rotat.'. The bottom entries are likewise 'Cels. 18°4 Rotunde | Reaum. 16°3 Magnetometer'.
Shelton entry at top reads '37 50' (i.e. 37'50"), not '+37.50'.
The boxed values 445.5 / 322.1 / 293.6 belong with the formulas 1/(r+m), 1/(r+m+1) and 1/(r+m+rm).
